GENA2122 · Meme warfare in the 2024 US election

Cats, context
& political
meaning

How does an entertaining image become a political message?

Start with a small change:
the same cat, a different caption.

GPT-generated teaching example. The repeated image is intentional.

The picture stays. Our reading changes.

Guiding question: How did cat imagery become material for political framing in Springfield in 2024?
01

Look at the two pictures. They use exactly the same cat. What changes is the caption, and that changes the situation we imagine. We might read the same expression as relief in one version and disbelief in the other. Neither response is built into the pixels alone.

These are teaching examples, not posts collected from a real meme community. They demonstrate an operation: giving a familiar image a new context. Our question is what happens when that new context is political. We will introduce a way to read memes, examine cat imagery in the 2024 Springfield controversy, then use a static classroom example to test the analysis.

Transition: First, what makes something an internet meme?

01 · Understanding memes

What makes an internet meme?

A family of related digital items, circulated, imitated and transformed by people.

Another teaching variant of the opening image.

01

Recognisable

Versions share elements of content, form or stance.

02

Remixable

People make versions in relation to other versions.

03

Circulated

Users copy, adapt and put the material to new uses.

Memes can be images, videos or sounds. Humour is common, but not required.

[1] Shifman (2013); explanatory interview with Shifman, Jenkins (2014). The three labels above are a teaching summary.
02

Following Limor Shifman, we focus on related digital items rather than treating the meme as a single isolated image. Versions can share content, form or stance. People create them with awareness of one another and circulate, imitate or transform them online.

The labels on this slide are a simple way to remember that account. A recognisable element lets people connect one version with another. Remixing allows a version to say something different. Circulation places those versions into social use. A widely shared image might remain unchanged; analysing a meme family also asks how different versions relate.

Memes are not limited to cats or still pictures. A sound, a repeated performance or a video format can also be used this way. Humour is frequent, but serious messages can participate in the same practices.

Transition: To explain a particular remix, we need to separate what stays from what changes.

01 · Understanding memes

Content, form and stance

GPT-generated teaching example.

Content

What is it about?

A change to the class schedule.

Form

How is it presented?

A reused cat image with a new caption.

Stance

What attitude does it invite?

Perhaps frustration or disbelief.
The audience still interprets it.

A remix can select, simplify and reframe an event—not just shorten it.

[1] Shifman (2013). Content, form and stance are analytical dimensions; they do not all have to change in each remix.
03

These three dimensions give us a practical method. Content asks what people or events the meme concerns. Form asks how it is presented: an image, text, layout, sound or performance. Stance asks about the attitude and relationship expressed through that use.

In our opening example, the general visual form stays stable while the caption changes the situation. That also makes a different attitude available to the viewer. It does not force every person to react in exactly the same way.

This is why describing meme-making only as compression is incomplete. A caption can remove context, select one concern or reverse an earlier meaning. Those are interpretive choices. The template may be familiar while the claim is new. In the case study, we will keep returning to the same questions: what remains recognisable, what context is added, and whose perspective becomes easier to see?

Transition: Those choices become politically significant when they concern public events and social groups.

01 · Understanding memes

Meme warfare and political meaning

Our working definition: repeated meme-making and circulation used to contest political narratives, group identities and attention.

01

Expression

“This is how I see
the event.”

02

Identification

“These are our people.
Those are the others.”

03

Contestation

“Our version should
define what happened.”

2008

Jenkins was already describing ordinary users manipulating and circulating political images.

This practice predates generative AI. Similar images alone do not establish central coordination.

[2] Jenkins (2008). The definition and three functions are the analytical framing used in this presentation.
04

A political meme can make an opinion visible, signal belonging or contest how an event should be understood. These are overlapping functions, not stages every meme must pass through. We use meme warfare as a working term for repeated contests over political narratives, identities and attention.

The metaphor of warfare needs care. One political joke does not establish a coordinated operation. Similar designs can emerge through imitation without a single director. Claims about coordination require evidence about the people and organisations involved.

There is also a historical continuity. In 2008, Henry Jenkins described ordinary people manipulating and circulating political images. Generative AI did not invent that participatory practice. Our 2024 case lets us examine how familiar practices of adaptation meet new image-making tools and a specific election controversy. One case will not establish a complete history of American political communication.

Transition: That brings us to Springfield, Ohio, in September 2024.

02 · The case

Ohio, United States · September 2024

Springfield

False allegations that Haitian immigrants were eating pets entered the US election debate.

The allegations lacked substantiating evidence. Cat imagery nevertheless became part of the political response.

GPT-generated conceptual illustration; not a historical post or video still.

Our question: How was entertaining cat imagery given political meaning?

[3] Tuquero, PolitiFact, 25 September 2024. The image illustrates the topic; the report supplies the event record.
05

The background can be stated briefly. During the 2024 election, false allegations about Haitian immigrants eating pets in Springfield circulated and entered political debate. PolitiFact documented how artificial images of cats and other animals became attached to that narrative.

The picture here is a newly generated illustration. It is not an original post, a historical video frame or evidence that the allegation occurred. The historical record comes from the reporting cited below.

We will examine two different uses: a video given a new caption, and a separate image used by a political account. The first helps us see recontextualisation; the second helps us analyse roles and the significance of the publisher.

Transition: We can begin with a political change that did not require making a new image.

02 · The case · Recontextualisation

A new caption changes the context

Earlier entertainment use

10 August 2024

The original video’s caption did not link the cats to Ohio.

Later political use

Documented in September

A repost connected the same video to the Springfield controversy.

Reported caption/context comparison. Both pictures are the same GPT-generated stand-in, not frames from the original video.

Our reading: a new context lets the material tell a political story.

[3] Tuquero (2024), tracing the original Instagram video and its Facebook reuse. Right-hand wording summarises the repost’s framing.
06

PolitiFact traced a video described as Navy SEAL Kittens to an Instagram post on August 10. The original caption did not associate it with Ohio. A later Facebook use connected that same material to cats taking back Springfield.

These two pictures are identical generated stand-ins. They help visualise the comparison, but they are not the historical video. The claim that the video was reused comes from the report.

Apply our framework. A recognisable visual remains. The caption adds a location and a political situation. It also supplies a way of interpreting the cats’ actions. The resulting political meaning depends on what the material is made to refer to, not simply on how the image was produced.

This is our close reading of that change. It does not tell us that every viewer accepted the underlying claim. To assess belief change, we would need different evidence.

Transition: A separate image from the same controversy makes political roles more explicit.

02 · The case · Framing and publication

Images assign political roles

GPT-generated conceptual reconstruction. Not the original post.

The animals

Positioned as objects of protection.

The political figure

Presented in the role of protector.

The publisher

A political account makes the political use explicit.

House Judiciary GOP posted an image of Trump holding a cat and a duck on 9 September 2024. This is a separate example, not a derivative of the kitten video.

Our reading: the image organises the controversy around “who protects whom”.

[3] Tuquero (2024), publication record. Role interpretation is our analysis. [4] Samaras (2026), abstract, provides related research on Springfield imagery.
07

The report documents a September 9 post by House Judiciary GOP showing Trump holding a cat and a duck. The illustration here recreates only that broad arrangement. It does not reproduce the original image’s details.

Our interpretation concerns roles. The animals become the objects of protection; the politician is positioned as their protector. The account matters because it places the image into explicit political communication. Rather than presenting a complete policy argument, the arrangement makes a particular relationship easy to recognise.

This is another image from the controversy, not a later stage in the military-kitten video’s production. We should not turn separate examples into an invented chain of influence.

Samaras’s 2026 study includes Springfield among the themes in a multimodal analysis of Musk’s posts. It provides related scholarly context; its abstract does not establish the effects of this specific post on voters.

Transition: We can now answer our opening question while keeping the limits of the evidence visible.

02 · The answer

Political meaning takes shape
through how images are used

Adaptation

A recognisable image can carry a new message.

Context

Captions connect images to events, roles and attitudes.

Circulation

Users and political accounts place images into public debate.

Where AI fits

AI can supply imagery. Recaptioning, framing and taking a stance do not depend on it.

What this case establishes

Documented uses and plausible readings.
It does not establish changed votes.

Synthesis of the framework [1–2] and the documented case [3]. Production, exposure, belief and voting are distinct outcomes.
08

Our answer has three parts. Adaptation preserves recognisable material while allowing a new message. Context links the material to an event and invites a stance. Circulation by users and political accounts places that use into public debate.

The historical point is limited but useful: a practice visible before generative AI was used within a particular 2024 election controversy, alongside generated imagery. The case does not establish that AI invented political memes or that greater image production necessarily produced greater persuasion.

We have evidence about uses and can offer readings of those uses. Exposure, belief change and voting would each require further evidence. That distinction completes the argument.

Transition: Let’s apply the method to a simple, fictional campus example.

03 · Static demonstration & discussion

Whose story does the meme tell?

One fictional event. The same image. Two different perspectives.

A · The announcement
Campus notice

The dining hall will stay open until 11 p.m. for a two-week trial.

The notice says nothing about staffing or shifts.
B · A student’s perspective
C · An employee’s perspective
01 · SELECTING INFORMATION

What does each version highlight, omit or assume?

Look beyond what the notice actually says.
02 · EXPRESSING A STANCE

Why does the same image invite different readings?

Who is speaking, and what matters to them?
03 · LOCATING AI’S ROLE

If AI makes a new cat, what changes—and what still depends on us?

Separate image production from framing.
All material on this slide is a fictional teaching example. Cat image generated with GPT. No live generation or audience devices required.
09

0:00–0:30 — Observe. Read the announcement and let the audience compare both versions. Say explicitly that the notice does not describe staffing arrangements. These are prepared fictional examples.

0:30–2:00 — Question 1. Invite one or two short responses. B foregrounds access to food. C foregrounds working time and suggests an implication that the notice itself does not establish. If the room is quiet, ask: “Does the announcement tell us whether existing workers will work longer?” Summarise: selecting information can also introduce assumptions.

2:00–3:30 — Question 2. Ask which words identify the speaker and their concern. Connect the replies to content, form and stance. The same image does not lock in the same interpretation. Welcome alternative readings and ask for the textual or visual detail behind them.

3:30–4:40 — Question 3. No generation is needed. Ask what a new AI image would actually alter. It might change visual details or the production process. Decisions about what to highlight, who is speaking and what the caption implies still need analysis. A generated variation alone would not establish increased persuasion.

4:40–5:00 — Close. “To understand a meme’s political meaning, ask what it shows, how it is rewritten, who uses it, and how it invites us to understand an event.”
